questions.q: Give an example of two OS design goals that may contradict one another.
questions.a: Efficiency (resource utilisation) vs user convenience/responsiveness. You can't optimise both: a supercomputer (expensive hardware) optimises utilisation, while a PC (cheap hardware) optimises convenience. Other pairs: fairness vs throughput (SJF maximises throughput but is unfair), and response time vs utilisation (a small RR quantum is responsive but wastes CPU on context switches).
questions.src: S-W1 'OS Goals', 'Design Trade-offs'; S-W7 'Pros and Cons'

mcq.q: According to the W1 slides, which two goals "cannot both be optimised"?
mcq.a: Efficiency (utilisation) and user convenience

mcq.q: Why does a supercomputer favour utilisation while a PC favours convenience?
mcq.a: Supercomputer hardware is expensive; PC hardware is cheap and the user's time matters more
w: Utilisation and convenience are the same thing on a PC

mcq.q: Which is an example of fairness conflicting with throughput?
mcq.a: SJF gives the best throughput/waiting time but can starve long jobs
w: FIFO gives the best throughput and is perfectly fair

questions.q: What is the difference between kernel and user mode? How does having two modes aid OS design?
questions.a:
Kernel mode: full access to hardware and all instructions (including privileged ones); a crash is catastrophic.
User mode: no direct hardware access, no privileged instructions (I/O, memory management); a crash only affects that process.
Why it helps: it protects the OS from errant users and processes from each other. User code must request services through system calls (traps), so the kernel controls all hardware access.

mcq.q: Which statement about user mode is correct?
mcq.a: It cannot execute privileged instructions such as I/O or memory management
w: It has full access to hardware
A crash in user mode brings down the whole system
Kernel code runs in user mode for speed

mcq.q: How does a user program get a kernel service?
mcq.a: Through a system call, which traps into kernel mode
w: By writing directly to device registers

mcq.q: The main design benefit of dual mode is:
mcq.a: Protecting the OS (and other processes) from errant user code
w: Allowing user code to manage page tables

questions.q: What is the difference between a trap and an interrupt?
questions.a:
Trap (exception/fault): internally generated, software-based, caused by the running instruction. Examples: system call, error (illegal instruction, div by zero, addressing violation), page fault.
Interrupt: externally generated, hardware-based, asynchronous. Examples: keyboard, disk operation complete, hardware timer (time slice).

mcq.q: Which pair of keywords did the lecturer use for traps?
mcq.a: Internally generated, software-based

mcq.q: A page fault is a(n):
mcq.a: Trap

mcq.q: Which of these is an interrupt?
mcq.a: The hardware timer expiring at the end of a time slice

questions.q: What are the ways to transfer control of the CPU to the OS? Why is a separate kernel stack generally used?
questions.a:
Ways: while a process runs the OS has lost control. It regains it via traps (system calls, errors, page faults) and interrupts (I/O devices, and especially the hardware timer, which enables preemptive multitasking).
Separate kernel stack (textbook reasoning): the user stack pointer can't be trusted (it may be invalid, corrupt, or full), and kernel data left on the user stack could be read or modified by user code, so a kernel stack is needed for reliability and protection/security.
questions.src: S-W2 'OS and Control?'; kernel stack: Tanenbaum (not in slides)

mcq.q: Which is NOT a way for the OS to regain control of the CPU?
mcq.a: The user process calling a normal library function like strlen()

mcq.q: Why use a separate kernel stack instead of the interrupted process's stack?
mcq.a: The user stack may be invalid or full, and kernel data left there could be read or modified by user code
w: Kernel stacks are faster because they're stored on disk
User stacks can't hold return addresses
To allow user code to call kernel functions directly

mcq.q: Which mechanism is most important for preemptive multitasking?
mcq.a: Hardware timer interrupt

questions.q: Two jobs each need 10 min of CPU and start simultaneously. With 50% I/O wait, how long until the last completes sequentially? In parallel?
questions.a:
Each job alone takes 20 min (10 CPU + 10 waiting).
Sequential: 20 + 20 = 40 min.
Parallel: CPU utilisation = 1 − pn = 1 − 0.5² = 0.75, shared between 2 jobs, so 0.375 CPU-min per minute each. 10 / 0.375 ≈ 26.7 min.

mcq.q: Sequentially, when does the last job finish?
mcq.a: 40 minutes

mcq.q: In parallel, roughly when does the last job finish?
mcq.a: ≈ 26.7 minutes

mcq.q: CPU utilisation with n processes each waiting on I/O a fraction p of the time is:
mcq.a: 1 − pⁿ

questions.q: What are multiprogramming, multitasking and multiprocessing? What's the difference?
questions.a:
Multiprogramming: several programs in memory share one CPU; when one blocks on I/O another runs. Goal: hardware utilisation, with no user interaction.
Multitasking/time-sharing: rapid switching between tasks (preemptive or cooperative), giving the illusion of parallelism for user experience.
Multiprocessing: multiple processing units, so true parallelism.

mcq.q: Which paradigm provides TRUE parallelism?
mcq.a: Multiprocessing

mcq.q: Multitasking's key goal is:
mcq.a: The illusion of parallelism and good user interaction via rapid switching
w: Maximum hardware utilisation with no interaction

mcq.q: Multiprogramming switches to another job when:
mcq.a: The current job blocks on I/O

questions.q: What is a process? What does it include? What is a PCB?
questions.a:
Process: a program in execution; a container holding everything needed to run a program; an entity with an address space and resources.
Includes: code (text), data, stack, open files, PC, registers, stack pointer.
PCB: the kernel data structure representing a process: state, PID, program counter, registers, scheduling info, memory structure (page/segment tables), open file table, accounting info. It's kept in kernel space and used to save and restore context on a context switch.
questions.src: S-W2 'What is a process', 'Process Control Block (PCB)', 'PCB: Other Fields'

mcq.q: Which is NOT typically stored in a PCB?
mcq.a: The source code of the program

mcq.q: Where is the PCB kept?
mcq.a: In kernel space, for protection

mcq.q: A process's memory has three main segments:
mcq.a: Text (code), data, stack

questions.q: What are the two models of IPC? Strengths and weaknesses of each?
questions.a:
Shared memory: + fast, convenient; − needs protection and synchronisation (race conditions).
Message passing: + no conflicts and no explicit synchronisation needed (the kernel passes messages), easy to implement; − slow (kernel on every message), only good for small amounts of data.

mcq.q: Which IPC model is fastest for large data?
mcq.a: Shared memory

mcq.q: Main weakness of shared memory:
mcq.a: Requires synchronisation/protection to avoid race conditions

mcq.q: Message passing is best for:
mcq.a: Small amounts of data, with no explicit synchronisation needed
w: Huge data transfers at maximum speed

questions.q: Describe the actions taken by a kernel to context-switch between processes.
questions.a:
1. Kernel gains control (timer interrupt, trap/system call, I/O block).
2. Save current process state into its PCB (PC, registers, SP, memory info), and update its state (Running → Ready/Blocked).
3. Scheduler picks the next ready process.
4. Load the new process's state from its PCB (including page table / memory mappings), set it to Running, return to user mode at its saved PC.
questions.src: S-W2 'Context Switch Using PCB'; S-W9 'Context Switch'

mcq.q: During a context switch, the current process's registers are saved to:
mcq.a: Its PCB

mcq.q: What decides which process runs next?
mcq.a: The scheduler/dispatcher, choosing from the ready queue
w: The process that was just interrupted

mcq.q: Why is the page table pointer part of the saved context?
mcq.a: Each process has its own address space; the same logical address maps to different frames
w: Page tables are shared by all processes
It isn't; page tables are global

questions.q: What resources are used when a thread is created? How do they differ from creating a process?
questions.a:
Thread: only a small private context: its own registers (incl. PC), stack, and TCB. It shares code, data, heap, open files, and address space with its process.
Process: needs a new PCB, a whole new address space, and a copy of the parent's context (fork duplicates the whole context including virtual memory, plus open files).
So threads are much cheaper to create and switch.
questions.src: S-W3 'Threads', 'Processes vs Threads', 'Threads: Benefits'; S-W2 'Fork Steps'

mcq.q: Which items are private to each thread?
mcq.a: Registers (PC) and stack

mcq.q: Why is thread creation cheaper than process creation?
mcq.a: Threads share the process's address space, code, data and files, so little new state is needed

mcq.q: fork() creating a process involves:
mcq.a: A new PCB and duplicating the parent's entire context, including virtual memory

questions.q: Explain what a race condition and a critical section are, and how they're related.
questions.a:
Race condition: shared data is read/written by multiple threads and the final result depends on the precise execution order (e.g. x++ and x-- each compile to LOAD/INC/STORE, which can interleave).
Critical section: the part of a program that accesses shared memory.
Relation: races happen when multiple threads are in their critical sections at the same time, so critical sections need mutual exclusion (plus progress and bounded wait).
questions.src: S-W4 'A Race Condition', 'Critical Region / Section', 'Critical Section Requirements'

mcq.q: A race condition is when:
mcq.a: The result depends on the exact order of execution of threads accessing shared data
w: Two threads run on different CPUs
A thread finishes faster than expected

mcq.q: Which is NOT one of the three critical-section requirements?
mcq.a: Preemption

mcq.q: Why does x++ cause a race?
mcq.a: It's not atomic: load, increment, store can interleave with another thread
w: It always triggers a page fault

questions.q: Give an example of an atomic machine instruction and explain what it does.
questions.a:
Test-and-Set: atomically sets a boolean lock to TRUE and returns the original value. while(TestAndSet(&lock)); spins until it returns false (the lock was free), then you enter the critical section; on exit set lock=false.
Swap / Compare-and-Swap: atomically exchanges two values (key=true; while(key) swap(&lock,&key);).
Both give mutual exclusion and progress, but not bounded waiting.
questions.src: S-W4 'Test and Set', 'Swap', 'Meet the Requirements?'; T-W12

mcq.q: TestAndSet(&lock) does what, atomically?
mcq.a: Sets lock to TRUE and returns its previous value
w: Sets lock to FALSE and returns TRUE
Increments lock and returns the new value

mcq.q: Which requirement do plain TestAndSet/Swap locks NOT satisfy?
mcq.a: Bounded waiting

mcq.q: With while(TestAndSet(&lock));, a thread enters the critical section when TestAndSet returns:
mcq.a: FALSE (the lock was free)

questions.q: What does "busy waiting" mean? What other kinds of waiting are there? Can busy waiting be avoided altogether?
questions.a:
Busy waiting (spinning): repeatedly looping and testing a condition (e.g. while(TestAndSet(&lock));), so it burns CPU doing no useful work. A spin lock is the typical case.
Other kind: blocking/sleeping: the thread sleeps on a wait queue and gives up the CPU until it's woken/signalled (semaphores with block/wakeup, condition variables, I/O wait).
Avoid altogether? No. Blocking primitives are built from atomic instructions, and guarding their own queue/count needs a very short spin (or disabled interrupts). It can only be minimised; modern mutexes spin briefly then sleep.
questions.src: S-W4 'Peterson's Solution', 'Mutex Locks...'; S-W5 'Building Semaphores'; T-W4

mcq.q: Busy waiting is undesirable mainly because:
mcq.a: The waiting thread consumes CPU cycles doing nothing useful

mcq.q: The alternative to busy waiting is:
mcq.a: Blocking: sleep on a wait queue and be woken later

mcq.q: Can busy waiting be eliminated completely?
mcq.a: No: implementing block/wakeup still needs a brief atomic spin to protect the queue, but it can be minimised
w: Yes, semaphores need no atomic operations
No, because blocking is impossible in modern OSes

questions.q: Explain why disabling interrupts is not appropriate for implementing synchronisation primitives in multiprocessor systems.
questions.a: Disabling interrupts only affects the CPU that executes it. Other cores keep running and can enter the same critical section at the same time, so there's no mutual exclusion. Disabling interrupts on all CPUs needs messages to every processor (slow), and letting user code disable interrupts is dangerous (the timer can't preempt, so the OS loses control). It only works on single-core machines.
questions.src: T-W4 ('it's not going to work for the multi-core system'); T-W3; S-W4

mcq.q: Disabling interrupts fails on multicore because:
mcq.a: Only the local CPU stops being interrupted; other cores can still enter the critical section

mcq.q: Where does disabling interrupts work as a (naive) solution?
mcq.a: Single-processor systems

mcq.q: An extra risk of letting user code disable interrupts:
mcq.a: The OS loses control: the timer can't preempt the process

questions.q: There are two operations on a semaphore. What are they, and how do you make them atomic?
questions.a:
P() / down / wait / acquire (Proberen, test): wait while s ≤ 0, then decrement. In the blocking version: count--; if(count<0) block.
V() / up / signal / release (Verhogen, increment): count++; if(count<=0) wake one waiter.
Atomicity: only one P or V at a time on a semaphore. Implementing them is itself a critical-section problem, solved with hardware atomic instructions (Test-and-Set/Swap) guarding the count and queue (or disabling interrupts on a uniprocessor).

mcq.q: P() on a semaphore:
mcq.a: Waits until the value is positive, then decrements it
w: Increments the value and wakes a waiter

mcq.q: How are P and V made atomic?
mcq.a: Using hardware atomic instructions like Test-and-Set to protect the semaphore's count and queue
w: By running them in user mode
By making the semaphore a float

mcq.q: In the blocking implementation, V() wakes a thread when, after incrementing, count is:
mcq.a: ≤ 0 (someone is still waiting)

questions.q: How does signal() for monitors differ from the corresponding semaphore operation?
questions.a:
Semaphore V() always increments the count, so it's remembered even if nobody is waiting, and a later P() won't block.
Monitor/condition-variable signal() only wakes a thread currently waiting on that condition. If none is waiting, the signal has no effect (it's lost). CVs have no value or history.
Course framing: "CV is about condition; semaphore is about integer."
questions.src: S-W5 'Condition Variables', 'CV vs Semaphore', 'Monitors'; lost-signal detail: Silberschatz

mcq.q: If signal() is called on a monitor condition with no waiting threads:
mcq.a: Nothing happens; the signal is lost

mcq.q: If V() is called on a semaphore with no waiting threads:
mcq.a: The semaphore value is incremented and remembered

mcq.q: The slides summarise the difference as:
mcq.a: CV is about a condition; a semaphore is about an integer
w: CV is hardware; semaphore is software
CV is for processes; semaphore for threads

questions.q: Explain the conditions required to create a deadlock.
questions.a:
All four must hold at the same time:
1. Mutual exclusion: at least one resource can't be shared.
2. Hold and wait: a process holds a resource while waiting for others.
3. No preemption: resources can't be taken from their holder.
4. Circular wait: A waits on B waits on C waits on A.

mcq.q: Which is NOT a necessary condition for deadlock?
mcq.a: Starvation

mcq.q: "A resource cannot be seized from its holder" is:
mcq.a: No preemption

mcq.q: How many of the four conditions must hold for deadlock?
mcq.a: All four, simultaneously

questions.q: 4 resources of the same type, shared by 3 processes, each needing at most 2. Show the system is deadlock-free.
questions.a:
Worst case: each process holds 1 and wants a 2nd, which is 3 held, so 1 is still free. Whichever process gets it reaches its max of 2, finishes, and releases 2, letting the others finish too. There's always a process that can complete, so no circular wait and no deadlock.
General rule: Σ(max − 1) + 1 ≤ resources → 3·1 + 1 = 4 ≤ 4.

mcq.q: In the worst case, how many resources remain free?
mcq.a: 1 (each process holds one)

mcq.q: Why can't deadlock occur?
mcq.a: The free resource lets one process reach its max of 2, finish, and release both

mcq.q: With 3 resources instead of 4 (same processes), could deadlock occur?
mcq.a: Yes: each could hold 1 and wait forever for a 2nd

questions.q: Explain deadlock prevention and deadlock avoidance.
questions.a:
Prevention: by design, break one of the four conditions so deadlock can never happen: e.g. request all resources at once (no hold-and-wait), preempt resources, or impose a global resource ordering (no circular wait). Downside: low utilisation and throughput.
Avoidance: allow the conditions but check each request dynamically and only grant it if the system stays in a safe state (a sequence exists in which all processes can finish). Needs a priori max-need info (Banker's/RAG). Unsafe ≠ deadlock. Cost: checking overhead.

mcq.q: Deadlock prevention works by:
mcq.a: Ensuring at least one of the four necessary conditions can never hold
w: Checking for a safe state on each request

mcq.q: Deadlock avoidance requires:
mcq.a: Advance knowledge of each process's maximum resource needs

mcq.q: An unsafe state means:
mcq.a: Deadlock is possible (not guaranteed)

questions.q: Compare the circular-wait scheme (prevention) with deadlock avoidance w.r.t. (a) runtime overhead and (b) throughput.
questions.a:
(a) Runtime overhead: circular-wait ordering is very low (just request in a fixed order, no runtime checks); avoidance is high (a safety check on every allocation, tracking allocations and max needs).
(b) Throughput: circular wait can be lower (resources grabbed in order, often early and held longer, which reduces concurrency); avoidance can be higher (it allows more concurrent allocations and only refuses unsafe ones).
questions.src: S-W6 'Deadlock Prevention' summary, 'Deadlock Avoidance'; comparison: Silberschatz

mcq.q: Which has the lower runtime overhead?
mcq.a: Circular-wait (resource ordering) prevention

mcq.q: Which typically allows higher throughput?
mcq.a: Deadlock avoidance: it permits more concurrent allocation

mcq.q: Why can resource ordering hurt throughput?
mcq.a: Processes must acquire resources in a fixed order, often earlier than needed, holding them longer
w: It requires a safety algorithm each request
It needs a priori max needs

questions.q: N processes are ready to run on a single processor. How many different schedules are possible?
questions.a: N! (N factorial): N choices for the first, N−1 for the second, and so on (each running to completion once).

mcq.q: How many schedules for N processes on one CPU?
mcq.a: N!

mcq.q: How many schedules for 4 processes?

questions.q: What would happen if a process appeared twice or more in the round-robin list? Any reason to allow it?
questions.a: It gets two (or more) quanta per round, so a bigger share of the CPU (2/(n+1) instead of 1/n). Reason: a simple way to implement priority/weighted share in round robin: more important processes get more turns.

mcq.q: A process listed twice in an RR queue will:
mcq.a: Get two quanta per round: a larger CPU share

mcq.q: A reason to allow duplicate entries:
mcq.a: To give higher priority/weight to important processes

questions.q: Explain how time quantum and context-switch time affect each other in round robin.
questions.a:
Large q → less responsive; RR degrades to FIFO (a thread waits up to q(n−1)).
Small q → more responsive, but context-switch overhead takes a bigger share (useful fraction ≈ q/(q+s)).
So q must be much larger than the context-switch time while still small enough for response time (typically 10–100 ms).

mcq.q: If q is very large, RR behaves like:
mcq.a: FIFO

mcq.q: If q is too small:
mcq.a: Most CPU time is wasted on context switching

mcq.q: The rule of thumb for q is:
mcq.a: Much longer than the context-switch time

questions.q: Explain the difference between preemptive and nonpreemptive scheduling. Give an example.
questions.a:
Non-preemptive: a process keeps the CPU until it finishes its burst or blocks. Examples: FIFO/FCFS, non-preemptive SJF.
Preemptive: the OS can take the CPU away (timer interrupt, or a higher-priority/shorter job arrives). Examples: Round Robin, SRTF, preemptive priority.

mcq.q: Which is a preemptive algorithm?
mcq.a: Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)

mcq.q: In non-preemptive scheduling a process gives up the CPU when:
mcq.a: It finishes its CPU burst or blocks

mcq.q: Round robin is preemptive because:
mcq.a: The process is preempted when its quantum expires
w: It runs the shortest job first

questions.q: Real-time system: two voice calls (period 5 ms, 1 ms CPU each) and one video stream (period 40 ms, 12 ms CPU). Schedulable?
questions.a:
Utilisation = Σ Cᵢ/Pᵢ = 1/5 + 1/5 + 12/40 = 0.2 + 0.2 + 0.3 = 0.7 ≤ 1, so schedulable.
(The formula is textbook; the course stresses that real-time means meeting deadlines/guarantees.)
questions.src: Tanenbaum periodic real-time condition; S-W7 'Scheduling Goals'

mcq.q: Total CPU utilisation for this system:
A periodic real-time system is schedulable (in this simple model) if:
mcq.a: Σ Cᵢ/Pᵢ ≤ 1

mcq.q: Key difference between real-time and interactive systems:
mcq.a: Real-time must guarantee deadlines

questions.q: Propose a scheduling algorithm that favours I/O-bound programs without starving CPU-bound programs.
questions.a: Multilevel feedback queue + aging. New jobs start in the top queue (high priority, short quantum). I/O-bound jobs block before their quantum ends, so they stay high and get fast response. CPU-bound jobs use their full quantum and get demoted to lower queues with longer quanta. Aging (promoting long-waiting jobs), or a guaranteed time share per level (e.g. 80/20), stops starvation.

mcq.q: Best fit for "favour I/O-bound, don't starve CPU-bound":
mcq.a: Multilevel feedback queue with aging
w: Fixed-priority with CPU-bound always lowest and no aging

mcq.q: In an MLFQ, a CPU-bound process that uses its full quantum is:
mcq.a: Demoted to a lower-priority queue

mcq.q: What prevents starvation in priority-based schemes?
mcq.a: Aging: increasing priority the longer a process waits

questions.q: One scheduling algorithm may decay into another under some circumstances. Give a couple of examples.
questions.a:
• RR with a very large quantum → FIFO.
• Priority with all-equal priorities → FIFO (or RR).
• SJF/SRTF with equal-length jobs → FIFO.
• Priority = 1/(next burst length) → SJF.
• MLFQ with a single queue → RR.
questions.src: S-W7 'Round Robin (RR)' ('q large → FIFO'); others: textbook

mcq.q: Round robin with a huge quantum becomes:
mcq.a: FIFO

mcq.q: Priority scheduling where priority = 1/predicted burst is:
mcq.a: SJF

mcq.q: SJF where all jobs have the same burst length behaves like:
mcq.a: FIFO

questions.q: Explain what dynamic loading and dynamic linking are.
questions.a:
Dynamic loading: a routine isn't loaded into memory until it's called; unused code stays on disk, which reduces memory use.
Dynamic linking: system libraries are linked at run time, not compile time. A small stub locates or loads the library routine when it's first called. Programs are smaller and one shared library copy serves all processes.

mcq.q: Dynamic loading means:
mcq.a: A routine is only loaded into memory when it is called
w: Libraries are linked at compile time
The whole program is loaded at start
Pages are swapped to disk on fault

mcq.q: In dynamic linking, the small piece of code that locates the library routine is the:
mcq.a: Stub

mcq.q: A key benefit of dynamic linking:
mcq.a: Smaller executables, and shared library code across processes

questions.q: What is the key function of the MMU? In memory protection, what is the limit register used for?
questions.a:
MMU: a hardware device that maps virtual/logical addresses to physical addresses at run time (e.g. physical = logical + relocation register). User programs never see physical addresses.
Limit register: holds the range (max logical address); every address is checked (logical < limit), otherwise trap. This keeps a process inside its own address space. (The relocation register holds the smallest physical address.)

mcq.q: The MMU's key function is:
mcq.a: Mapping logical (virtual) addresses to physical addresses at run time

mcq.q: A process is loaded at physical 14000–15000. The limit register holds:
If a logical address ≥ limit:
mcq.a: A trap (addressing error) to the OS

questions.q: Holes in order: 10, 4, 20, 18, 7, 9, 12, 15 MB. Requests 15, 10, 5 MB. Which hole for First Fit and Best Fit?
questions.a:
First Fit: 15 → 20 MB hole (5 left); 10 → 10 MB; 5 → the 5 MB leftover of the 20 MB hole (the 4 MB hole is too small). (If leftovers are ignored: 18 MB.)
Best Fit: 15 → 15 MB; 10 → 10 MB; 5 → 7 MB.

mcq.q: First Fit: where does the 15 MB request go?
mcq.a: 20 MB hole

mcq.q: Best Fit: where does the 5 MB request go?
mcq.a: 7 MB hole

mcq.q: Best Fit: where does the 15 MB request go?
mcq.a: 15 MB hole

questions.a:
Rule: offset < length → base + offset, else trap.
(a) 500<600 → 719
(b) 30≥14 → trap
(c) 400≥100 → trap
(d) 800≥580 → trap
(e) 12<96 → 1964

mcq.q: Physical address of (0, 500)?
Physical address of (4, 12)?
Result of (1, 30)?
mcq.a: Trap: offset 30 ≥ length 14

questions.q: What are a page and a frame?
questions.a:
Page: a fixed-size block of logical memory.
Frame: a block of physical memory of the same size.
The page table maps page number → frame number; a program of n pages needs n free frames (not necessarily contiguous).

mcq.q: A frame is:
mcq.a: A fixed-size block of physical memory
w: A fixed-size block of logical memory

mcq.q: Pages and frames are:
mcq.a: The same size

questions.q: Physical memory is 2⁸ bytes. For physical address 11000001, what is the frame number if frame numbers use 2, 3, and 4 bits?
questions.a:
High bits = frame number, the rest = offset.
2 bits: 11 = 3 (offset 1, frame size 64 B)
3 bits: 110 = 6 (offset 1, 32 B)
4 bits: 1100 = 12 (offset 1, 16 B)

mcq.q: Frame number with 3-bit frame numbers?
Frame size with 4-bit frame numbers (2⁸ B memory)?
mcq.a: 16 bytes

mcq.q: Frame number with 2-bit frame numbers?

questions.q: What is a TLB? Why is it needed?
questions.a:
TLB (Translation Look-aside Buffer): a small, fast, fully associative hardware cache of recent page → frame translations; all entries are compared in parallel (64–1024 entries).
Why: the page table lives in memory, so every access would need 2 memory accesses (page table + data). The TLB avoids the page-table access in most cases.

mcq.q: The TLB caches:
mcq.a: Recent page-number → frame-number translations

mcq.q: Without a TLB, each memory reference costs:
mcq.a: Two memory accesses (page table + data)

mcq.q: TLB lookups are fast because:
mcq.a: All entries are compared in parallel (associative)

questions.q: Explain how the TLB works on a hit and on a miss.
questions.a:
Hit: page number p is in the TLB, so the frame f comes straight from it; physical = f + offset (one memory access).
Miss: p isn't in the TLB, so walk the page table in memory (via PTBR) to get f, form the address, and insert (p, f) into the TLB (replacing an entry if full). If the PTE is invalid, that's a page fault.
questions.src: S-W9 'Paging Hardware with TLB', 'Handling a Miss'

mcq.q: On a TLB miss the hardware/OS:
mcq.a: Looks up the page table in memory and then adds the translation to the TLB
w: Reads the page from disk immediately

mcq.q: On a TLB hit the frame number comes from:
mcq.a: The TLB entry directly

mcq.q: A TLB miss where the page-table entry is marked invalid leads to:
mcq.a: A page fault

questions.q: 64-bit machine, 4 KB pages, two-level page table with all tables having the same number of PTEs. How many page tables, and how many PTEs per table?
questions.a:
Offset = 12 bits (4 KB = 2¹²). 64 − 12 = 52, split equally: p1 = 26, p2 = 26.
PTEs per table = 2²⁶ (≈67M).
Number of tables = 1 outer + 2²⁶ inner = 2²⁶ + 1.

mcq.q: How many offset bits for 4 KB pages?
PTEs per page table?
mcq.a: 2²⁶

mcq.q: Total number of page tables?
mcq.a: 2²⁶ + 1

questions.q: Discuss the relationship between the File Control Block, system-wide open file table, and per-process open file table.
questions.a:
FCB (on disk, e.g. an inode): permissions, size, dates, pointers to data blocks.
System-wide open file table (memory): a copy of the FCB of each open file + an open count.
Per-process open file table: entries pointing to the system-wide entry (plus per-process position); the fd indexes it.
open(): if not in the system-wide table, search the directory and load the FCB, then add a per-process entry and return the fd. close(): remove the per-process entry and decrement the count; at 0, write metadata back and remove the system-wide entry.

mcq.q: The system-wide open file table contains:
mcq.a: A copy of each open file's FCB plus an open count

mcq.q: A per-process open file table entry contains:
mcq.a: A pointer to the system-wide table entry
w: A full copy of the file

mcq.q: When the last process closes a file:
mcq.a: Metadata is written back and the system-wide entry is removed
w: The FCB is erased from disk

questions.q: A file varies between 4 KB and 4 MB. Which allocation scheme (contiguous, linked, indexed) is most efficient? Justify.
questions.a:
Indexed (ideally the combined/UFS scheme).
• Contiguous: must know or reserve the max size (wasting space while small); growing may need relocation; external fragmentation/compaction.
• Linked: grows fine, but direct access is slow (follow pointers) and it's unreliable (one bad pointer loses the rest).
• Indexed: grows block by block, no external fragmentation, supports sequential and direct access. 4 KB blocks with 4 B pointers give 1024 pointers = 4 MB, so one index block (or UFS direct + single indirect) covers it.

mcq.q: Best scheme for a file that grows from 4 KB to 4 MB?
mcq.a: Indexed allocation

mcq.q: Main problem with contiguous allocation here:
mcq.a: Must know/reserve the max size; growth causes relocation and external fragmentation

mcq.q: Main problem with linked allocation:
mcq.a: Direct access needs many I/Os, and one corrupt pointer loses the rest

questions.q: In general, what are the considerations when choosing a file allocation strategy?
questions.a:
• Access pattern: sequential vs direct/random.
• File size & growth: known/fixed vs dynamic.
• Space efficiency/fragmentation: external fragmentation and compaction; pointer/index overhead.
• Performance: number of disk seeks/I/Os per access (contiguous is best; FAT is cacheable).
• Reliability: corrupted pointers.
• Complexity/overhead of index structures and levels.
questions.src: S-W11 'Space Management' (best use of space, performance, reliability)

mcq.q: Which is NOT a main consideration for file allocation?
mcq.a: The CPU scheduling algorithm

mcq.q: If files are mostly read randomly, avoid:
mcq.a: Linked allocation

questions.q: Explain how FAT works.
questions.a: FAT (File Allocation Table) is linked allocation with all the links kept together in one table at the start of the volume, indexed by block number. The directory entry stores the first block; each FAT entry holds the next block number, ending with an EOF marker. It's faster and cacheable (the table can sit in memory, so direct access is just table lookups). To add a block: find a free entry, link it from the old EOF, and mark it EOF.

mcq.q: In FAT, the directory entry stores:
mcq.a: The block number of the file's first block
w: All block numbers of the file

mcq.q: Each FAT entry contains:
mcq.a: The number of the next block in the file (or EOF)

mcq.q: FAT's advantage over plain linked allocation:
mcq.a: Links are in one table that can be cached, so traversal is faster

questions.q: Where do you want to place the bit map? Explain why.
questions.a: Keep it on disk (volume control block/superblock area) so free-space info is persistent, and cache it in main memory for speed: finding free or contiguous blocks then needs no disk I/O (the CPU scans it a word at a time). 1 TB / 4 KB = 2²⁸ bits = 32 MB, which is affordable to cache. Trade-off: the in-memory copy must be written back carefully so a crash doesn't leave the disk copy inconsistent.
questions.src: S-W11 'On-Disk Structures', 'Bit map'; T-W12; caching trade-off: Silberschatz

mcq.q: Best placement for the free-space bit map:
mcq.a: Stored on disk, with a cached copy in main memory
w: Only in the per-process open file table

mcq.q: Why cache it in memory?
mcq.a: Fast lookup of free/contiguous blocks without disk I/O
w: The bitmap can't be stored on disk

mcq.q: Bitmap size for a 1 TB disk with 4 KB blocks:
mcq.a: 32 MB (2²⁸ bits)
